```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
options(cli.num_colors = 1, width = 80)
set.seed(1)
```

```{r setup}
library(yourhonor)
```

An LLM judge is a measurement instrument. Before its scores drive a launch,
ranking, or regression gate, we need evidence about agreement with humans,
class-specific errors, bias sensitivity, and repeatability. `yourhonor` assembles
that evidence, but it does not invent a universal definition of "good enough."

This walkthrough audits **one** judge end to end. Every piece of evidence is
tagged with the same `audit_id`, and `report()` only binds evidence that shares
that tag. The judge is synthetic, so no model is called, but it has a flaw
that a real judge might have: it reads long answers as more complete than short
ones. The audit is designed to find that flaw.

## Build a gold set

A calibration set needs stable item IDs, content the judge may see, and blind
human labels. This synthetic example makes the relationship between answer text
and labels explicit.

```{r}
labels <- sample(c("I", "P", "C"), 90, replace = TRUE, prob = c(.2, .3, .5))
answer_text <- ifelse(
  labels == "C", "This answer fully resolves the support question.",
  ifelse(
    labels == "P", "This answer helps but omits an important step.",
    "This answer is unrelated to the support question."
  )
)
answer_text <- sprintf("Synthetic case %03d: %s", seq_along(answer_text), answer_text)
gold <- tibble::tibble(
  id = sprintf("item-%03d", seq_along(labels)),
  input = answer_text,
  target = "Does the answer correctly and completely resolve the question?",
  human_label = labels
)
```

## Use a blind judge contract

When a live judge is supplied, `input_cols` is required. The function receives
only a generated `.item_id` and those declared columns. Human labels are never
passed to it. A keyed data-frame result is safest because row reordering becomes
detectable.

The judge below grades by keyword, adds a little random error so that repeated
runs are not identical, and carries the deliberate flaw: any input longer than
200 characters is graded one level more generously.

```{r}
toy_judge <- function(data) {
  label <- ifelse(
    grepl("fully resolves", data$input), "C",
    ifelse(grepl("omits", data$input), "P", "I")
  )
  # The flaw under audit: long answers look more complete to this judge.
  long <- nchar(data$input) > 200
  label[long & label == "P"] <- "C"
  label[long & label == "I"] <- "P"
  # A small amount of run-to-run judge error.
  change <- runif(nrow(data)) < 0.08
  label[change] <- sample(c("I", "P", "C"), sum(change), replace = TRUE)
  tibble::tibble(.item_id = data$.item_id, label = label)
}

cal <- calibrate_judge(
  gold,
  judge = toy_judge,
  input_cols = c("input", "target"),
  id_col = "id",
  label_levels = c("I", "P", "C"),
  scale = "ordinal",
  n_boot = 200,
  seed = 1,
  provenance = list(model = "synthetic", prompt_version = "v1"),
  audit_id = "synthetic-judge-v1"
)
cal
```

The gold inputs are all shorter than 200 characters, so calibration alone
cannot see the flaw. That is the point of running probes as well.

Items are shuffled before grading and the judge sees a fresh key. The result
keeps both: `items$.item_id` is the source-row key and `items$.judge_item_id`
is the key the judge saw, so judge-side logs can be joined back without
un-blinding the run.

```{r}
head(cal$items[, c(".item_id", ".judge_item_id", "human_label", "judge_label")])
```

`agreement()` returns chance-corrected estimates and bootstrap intervals. A
single-class sample is reported as insufficient variation rather than perfect
agreement. For ordered labels, set `scale = "ordinal"` and declare the label
order; weighted agreement then distinguishes adjacent from extreme mistakes. A
zero-width bootstrap at empirically perfect agreement is flagged unreliable
rather than treated as proof of population-perfect agreement.

```{r}
agreement(cal)
```

Called on a calibration object, `agreement()` inherits the stored
`conf_level`, `n_boot`, and `seed`, so overriding one setting keeps the
others comparable with the original run.

## Inspect rare-class behavior

Aggregate agreement can look excellent while a judge misses every example in a
rare, important class. Inspect the confusion matrix and the per-class intervals.

```{r}
confusion(cal, normalize = "row")
confusion_metrics(cal)
```

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE), fig.width = 5, fig.height = 4}
plot_confusion(cal)
```

The gold set above is balanced enough that this is not dramatic. Here is the
failure mode at its worst: 990 acceptable answers, 10 incorrect ones, and a
judge that misses nine of the ten incorrect answers while getting almost every
acceptable answer right.

```{r}
human <- c(rep("C", 990), rep("I", 10))
judge <- human
judge[1:5] <- "I"      # five false alarms
judge[991:999] <- "C"  # nine of ten incorrect answers waved through
rare <- tibble::tibble(human_label = human, judge_label = judge)
rare_cal <- calibrate_judge(rare, label_levels = c("I", "C"), n_boot = 200, seed = 1)
rare_cal
confusion_metrics(rare_cal)
```

Gwet's AC1 is almost perfect because the prevalent class dominates; kappa is
near zero because the judge adds almost nothing over "always say C". Neither
coefficient is the quantity that matters here. A policy with a recall floor for
`I` names the failure directly:

```{r}
rare_policy <- acceptance_policy(
  min_agreement_lower = 0.75,
  min_n = 100,
  min_class_n = 10,
  min_recall = c(I = 0.90, C = 0.90),
  max_missing_rate = 0.01,
  max_pairwise_disagreement = NULL
)
rare_report <- report(rare_cal, policy = rare_policy)
rare_report$decision
rare_report$checks[, c("check", "status", "value", "op", "threshold")]
```

## Multiple human raters

With multiple raters, each item's reference label is the modal (most frequent)
human label. An item whose top labels tie has no consensus; it is counted in
`n_consensus_ties` and excluded from the judge-versus-consensus evidence. With
two raters every disagreement is a tie, so the judge is scored only on items
the humans agreed about, which is optimistic. `per_rater_agreement` is the
all-items counterpart, and human-human reliability is a benchmark, not a
ceiling: agreement with a consensus can exceed pairwise human agreement.

```{r}
multi <- tibble::tibble(
  h1 = c("C", "C", "P", "I", "C", "P", "I", "C"),
  h2 = c("C", "P", "P", "I", "C", "C", "I", "C"),
  h3 = c("C", "C", "P", "P", "C", "P", "I", "C"),
  judge_label = c("C", "C", "C", "I", "C", "P", "P", "C")
)
multi_cal <- calibrate_judge(
  multi,
  human_cols = c("h1", "h2", "h3"),
  label_levels = c("I", "P", "C"),
  scale = "ordinal",
  n_boot = 100,
  seed = 1
)
multi_cal$n_consensus_ties
multi_cal$human_reliability
multi_cal$per_rater_agreement
```

## Probe pointwise bias

Pointwise probes score control and treatment rows in one randomized batch.
The verbosity probe pads each answer with filler; the self-preference and
bandwagon probes prepend a short framing sentence. `no_signal` means no
directional effect was detected by that probe; it is not a claim that bias is
absent.

```{r}
bias <- probe_bias(
  gold,
  toy_judge,
  input_cols = c("input", "target"),
  probes = c("verbosity", "self_preference", "bandwagon"),
  seed = 1,
  audit_id = "synthetic-judge-v1"
)
bias[, c("probe", "flip_rate", "directional_rate", "direction", "p_value_adj", "verdict")]
```

The padded answers cross the judge's 200-character threshold, so the verbosity
probe finds the flaw: labels move towards the perturbed (longer) version. The
short framing prefixes do not, so those probes report `no_signal`. A `BIAS`
verdict needs both a small adjusted p-value and a `directional_rate` above
`flip_threshold`; a large but balanced `flip_rate` is reported but never
flagged.

Missingness is reported on two denominators. `missing_rate` is the share of
individual judgments that came back `NA` and is the quantity a policy gates;
`unscored_rate` is the share of items that could not be scored, which for the
position probe also includes within-condition ties.

```{r}
bias[, c("probe", "n_scored", "n_unscored", "unscored_rate", "missing_rate")]
```

Position bias uses a separate structured API for a *pairwise* judge. Source
columns are swapped and shown to the judge only as neutral `.candidate_1` and
`.candidate_2` slots, then display choices are mapped back to stable candidate
identity. A pairwise judge is a different instrument from the pointwise judge
audited above, so it gets its own `audit_id`.

```{r}
pairs <- tibble::tibble(
  question = c("2 + 2?", "Capital of France?"),
  candidate_a = c("4", "Paris"),
  candidate_b = c("5", "Berlin")
)
always_first <- function(data) rep("A", nrow(data))
position <- probe_position(
  pairs,
  always_first,
  candidate_a_col = "candidate_a",
  candidate_b_col = "candidate_b",
  context_cols = "question",
  repeats = 2,
  seed = 1,
  audit_id = "pairwise-judge-v1"
)
position[, c("probe", "flip_rate", "position_preference", "direction", "verdict")]
```

Every item flipped with the display order and the preference is entirely for
the first slot, yet the verdict is `no_signal`: two items cannot reach
significance in a sign test. A real position audit needs a proper item count,
which is what `min_probe_n` in a policy enforces.

Because its `audit_id` differs, `report()` refuses to bind this evidence to the
pointwise calibration rather than silently assessing two judges as one:

```{r, error = TRUE}
report(cal, bias = position)
```

## Measure repeatability

The primary stability quantity is mean pairwise disagreement across runs. Its
interval is a hybrid: the percentile item bootstrap widened to include a Wilson
score interval for the mean per-item disagreement, so a sample with no observed
disagreement never yields a zero-width interval. The Wilson bound usually sets
both ends once there are more than two runs; the interval can only widen, never
narrow. The any-flip rate is also shown but is explicitly tied to the chosen
number of runs.

```{r}
stability <- test_retest(
  gold,
  toy_judge,
  input_cols = c("input", "target"),
  n_runs = 5,
  label_levels = c("I", "P", "C"),
  n_boot = 200,
  seed = 1,
  audit_id = "synthetic-judge-v1"
)
stability
```

## Turn evidence into an explicit decision

`report()` is descriptive unless it receives an acceptance policy. Policy checks
use confidence bounds and distinguish failure, missing evidence, and statistical
indeterminacy. Thresholds that only apply inside a gate (`max_pairwise_disagreement`
for stability, `required_probes` for bias) must be supplied with that gate and
are rejected without it, so a policy never carries a threshold the assessment
does not read.

```{r}
policy <- acceptance_policy(
  min_agreement_lower = 0.75,
  min_n = 75,
  min_class_n = 10,
  min_recall = c(I = 0.80, P = 0.75, C = 0.85),
  max_missing_rate = 0.01,
  max_pairwise_disagreement = 0.10,
  min_stability_n = 75,
  min_stability_runs = 3,
  max_stability_missing_rate = 0.01,
  required_probes = c("verbosity", "self_preference", "bandwagon"),
  min_probe_n = 50,
  max_probe_flip_rate = 0.10,
  max_probe_directional_rate = 0.10,
  max_probe_missing_rate = 0.01,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  coefficient = "gwet_ac2"
)
verdict <- report(cal, bias = bias, stability = stability, policy = policy)
verdict
```

`report()` returns a `yourhonor_report` whichever `output` you choose; `output`
only sets the default rendering. `verdict$decision` is the overall outcome,
`verdict$checks` holds one row per check with the observed `value`, the
comparison `op`, and the numeric `threshold`, and
`format(verdict, output = "md")` gives the Markdown lines.

```{r}
verdict$decision
verdict$checks[verdict$checks$status != "PASS", c("check", "status", "value", "op", "threshold")]
```

The outcome may be `PASS`, `FAIL`, `NOT_ASSESSED`, or `INDETERMINATE`. That is
intentional: absence of a probe and an underpowered probe are different facts.
Here the verbosity flaw fails both verbosity checks (the flip-rate interval and
the directional interval both sit above the 0.10 ceiling), while the small gold
set leaves several other checks `INDETERMINATE` rather than `PASS`: their
intervals overlap the threshold, so the evidence neither clears nor fails it.

## Write an artifact

`write_audit()` writes the same assessment as a Markdown report or as a
versioned JSON summary (`yourhonor.audit.v1`). An existing file is never
replaced unless `overwrite = TRUE`, so a re-run cannot clobber an earlier audit.

```{r}
path <- tempfile("judge-audit-", fileext = ".json")
write_audit(cal, path, bias = bias, stability = stability, policy = policy)
```

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("jsonlite", quietly = TRUE)}
audit <- jsonlite::read_json(path)
audit$decision
names(audit)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
unlink(path)
```

The JSON artifact contains aggregate calibration evidence, policy checks, and
provenance at full numeric precision, with `null` for every absent value.
Calibration item rows are omitted, but caller-supplied provenance is written
verbatim; keep secrets and raw item content out of provenance fields.

## Reuse vitals scores

`audit_vitals()` reads `task$get_samples()$score` and joins human labels by ID;
it does not invoke the scorer again. A multi-epoch vitals task must be filtered
to one epoch for calibration because repeated grades are not independent gold
items. `stability_vitals()` can reuse epochs only after verifying that every
judge-visible content column stayed invariant. The chunk below is not run; it
needs a graded `vitals::Task` and a human review table.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
human_review <- tibble::tibble(id = review$id, human_label = review$label)
cal <- audit_vitals(
  task,
  human_labels = human_review,
  label_levels = c("I", "P", "C"),
  scale = "ordinal",
  provenance = list(judge_prompt = "grader-v3"),
  audit_id = "support-judge-v3-gold-2026-08",
  seed = 1
)
stability <- stability_vitals(
  task,
  content_cols = c("input", "target", "result"),
  label_levels = c("I", "P", "C"),
  weights = "ordinal",
  audit_id = "support-judge-v3-gold-2026-08",
  seed = 1
)
write_audit(cal, "judge-audit.json", policy = policy, format = "json", overwrite = TRUE)
```

## Statistical scope

The item bootstrap and exact class intervals assume independent sampling units.
Do not count repeated templates, users, conversations, or epochs as independent
items. Use a frozen, representative, held-out calibration set that was not used
to tune the judge or prompt, and record the data split/version/hash plus the
model and prompt versions in `provenance`. Confidence levels describe each
interval, not a simultaneous band over every estimate. This synthetic vignette
demonstrates APIs; it is not deployment evidence.
